thread.title: Tesla, the Saudi Prince and the Stalled Aramco IPO

author: Crystal Kim
title: Tesla, the Saudi Prince and the Stalled Aramco IPO
text:
A newly licensed Saudi motorist Photo: AMER HILABI/AFP/Getty Images By Crystal Kim Updated Aug. 23, 2018 5:39 p.m. ET Changing the world is hard. Just ask Elon Musk and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
With Tesla (TSLA), Musk, the company’s CEO, has been trying to reinvent just what a car can be— but has run into headwinds as he tries to bring his vision to the masses. Prince Mohammed has similar ambitions for Saudi Arabia, but if reports that plans for the initial public offering of that nation’s oil giant, Saudi Aramco, are on hold turn out to be true, he could be running into obstacles of his own.
Tesla and Saudi Arabia are linked by more than just the ambitions of their wealthy leaders. When Musk tweeted that he had secured the funding to take Tesla private, he was referring to Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, or PIF, according to his own blog post . The PIF has been central to the prince’s plan to modernize the country, and a potential Tesla deal is just the kind of forward-focused investment it’s looking to make for the future. (It also has a stake in Uber Technologies.)
But that’s just a sideshow to the centerpiece of Prince Mohammed’s plan: The IPO of Aramco. The prince laid out a diversification plan, dubbed Vision 2030, to shift the country’s economy away from oil dependence and modernize it. But the outlook of that plan has been muddied. On Wednesday, news broke that Saudi Arabia called off plans to take the oil giant public. And the Aramco IPO—projected to be valued at $2.5 trillion, twice that of Apple (AAPL)—was supposed to play a critical role in raising the sovereign-wealth fund’s assets under management to $400 billion by 2020 from its current $250 billion. With the IPO on ice, the future of the PIF and the prince’s Vision 2030 plans look uncertain.
On Thursday, the Saudi energy minister, Khalid al-Falih, denied the cancellation of the IPO . In a statement to the Saudi Press Agency, he said: “The government remains committed to the IPO of Saudi Aramco at a time of its own choosing when conditions are optimum.”
Saudi Arabia, however, has been looking at other sources of financing, says Helima Croft, head of commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets. “Now the talk is around tapping the international bond markets, raising billions of dollars via Aramco bond sales,” says Croft, who wasn’t surprised by the news. “Aramco could use the proceeds to buy out the PIF’s 70% stake in the petrochemical producer Sabic, which the government hopes will generate some $70 billion.”
That’s how Saudi Arabia accounts for some of the money that the Aramco IPO was supposed to bring, but not all of it. While the funding shift makes the Aramco IPO less important to government’s strategic plans, it remains to be seen where the rest of the financing will come from.
The delays with the IPO also bring into question other parts of the Vision 2030 plan and its implementation. Sure, the prince has made great strides in regulatory issues and bankruptcy law. There are women driving. The power of the religious police has been curtailed. But at the same time, Saudi Arabia and the prince will be judged on their ability to generate the millions of new jobs necessary to keep young Saudis employed, and where the PIF makes investments will shine on a light on how it will be able to deliver what the Saudis need.
“The government will have to come out and make core projections on Vision 2030 and retake the narrative,” says Croft. “Until then we have to wonder if these delays are the growing pains of a young man trying to rebuild a country or a sign that he’s reached the limits of what can be accomplished in the near term.”
The Tesla chief and the crown prince appear to have a lot in common.
